osces.title: Peripartum Cardiomyopathy - Heart Failure in Late Pregnancy

clinical_scenario.presenting_complaint: Worsening shortness of breath at 36 weeks gestation
clinical_scenario.history_of_presenting_complaint: Sarah is 36 weeks pregnant with her second child. She has developed progressive dyspnoea over the past 2 weeks, initially on exertion but now also occurring at rest. She needs 3 pillows to sleep comfortably and wakes gasping for air. She has noticed bilateral ankle swelling worse than her first pregnancy. She reports a dry cough at night and reduced exercise tolerance - unable to climb stairs without stopping. No chest pain, palpitations or syncope. Her first pregnancy was uncomplicated.
clinical_scenario.past_medical_history: Gestational diabetes current pregnancy (diet controlled), Iron deficiency anaemia, Previous uncomplicated vaginal delivery 3 years ago
clinical_scenario.medications: Elevit prenatal vitamins, Ferrous sulfate 325mg daily
clinical_scenario.social_history: Never smoked, No alcohol during pregnancy, Lives with husband, Good family support
clinical_scenario.family_history: Mother has type 2 diabetes, Father has hypertension, No family history of cardiomyopathy or sudden cardiac death

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP elevated 8cm above sternal angle, Displaced apex beat 6th intercostal space anterior axillary line, S3 gallop present, Soft systolic murmur at apex
examination_findings.respiratory: Bibasal fine inspiratory crackles to mid-zones bilaterally
examination_findings.peripheral: Bilateral pitting oedema to mid-calf, Cool peripheries with prolonged capillary refill 3 seconds
examination_findings.obstetric: Gravid uterus consistent with 36 weeks, Cephalic presentation, FHR 140 bpm regular

investigations.result: Sinus tachycardia 110 bpm, Left atrial enlargement, Non-specific ST-T wave changes in lateral leads
investigations.interpretation: Consistent with left ventricular strain pattern

investigations.result: 856 pg/mL
45 ng/L
LVEF 35%, LV end-diastolic dimension 58mm, Global hypokinesis, Moderate mitral regurgitation, No pericardial effusion
investigations.interpretation: Moderate-severe LV systolic dysfunction consistent with peripartum cardiomyopathy

investigations.result: Cardiomegaly with cardiothoracic ratio 0.58, Pulmonary vascular congestion, Small bilateral pleural effusions
Hb 95 g/L, MCV 72 fL, Platelets 185 x10^9/L, WCC 11.2 x10^9/L
investigations.interpretation: Iron deficiency anaemia contributing to symptoms

tasks.task: Explain the diagnosis of peripartum cardiomyopathy to Sarah
tasks.expected_response: Sarah, you have developed a condition called peripartum cardiomyopathy, which is heart failure that develops in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months after delivery. Your heart muscle has become weakened and isn't pumping blood effectively, causing fluid to build up in your lungs and legs. This is a serious condition that needs immediate treatment, but many women recover their heart function with proper management.

tasks.task: Outline immediate management plan
tasks.expected_response: Immediate admission to high-dependency unit for cardiac monitoring. Start frusemide 40mg IV for diuresis with strict fluid balance monitoring. Commence hydralazine 25mg TDS for afterload reduction as it's safe in pregnancy. Avoid ACE inhibitors and ARBs as they're teratogenic. Continuous CTG monitoring for fetal wellbeing. Liaise with obstetric team for delivery planning - may need urgent caesarean section if maternal condition deteriorates.

tasks.task: Discuss delivery timing and mode
tasks.expected_response: Given your moderate-severe heart failure at 36 weeks, we need to plan for delivery soon as this will improve your cardiac function. The timing depends on your response to medical therapy over next 24-48 hours. If you stabilize, we may attempt vaginal delivery with epidural for pain relief and assisted second stage to minimize cardiac stress. If you deteriorate or don't respond to treatment, caesarean section under regional anaesthesia would be safer. The neonatal team will be present as baby may need special care nursery admission.

tasks.task: Counsel about breastfeeding considerations
tasks.expected_response: Breastfeeding with peripartum cardiomyopathy requires careful consideration. Many heart failure medications like ACE inhibitors, which you'll need postpartum, aren't compatible with breastfeeding. Bromocriptine, which can help cardiac recovery, completely suppresses lactation. The physical demands of breastfeeding may also strain your heart during recovery. We'll discuss formula feeding options and provide lactation suppression if needed. Your cardiac recovery is the priority to ensure you can care for your baby long-term.

tasks.task: Explain prognosis and follow-up requirements
tasks.expected_response: About 50% of women with peripartum cardiomyopathy recover normal heart function within 6 months with treatment. You'll need regular cardiology follow-up with repeat echocardiograms at 6 weeks, 3 months and 6 months postpartum. Long-term medications include ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers and possibly spironolactone. Future pregnancies carry a 30-50% recurrence risk with higher mortality if heart function doesn't fully recover. We strongly recommend contraception counseling before discharge.

tasks.task: Address Sarah's concerns about caring for her toddler and newborn
tasks.expected_response: I understand this is overwhelming with a 3-year-old at home and a new baby coming. Your heart condition means you'll need significant help initially - consider family support or home help services through maternal child health. Limit physical activities like lifting your toddler or climbing stairs. Arrange baby equipment on one level of your home. Your husband or support person should handle night feeds initially to ensure you get adequate rest for cardiac recovery. Social work can help arrange practical supports through Centrelink carer payments.

learning_objectives: Recognize peripartum cardiomyopathy presentation in late pregnancy
Select pregnancy-safe cardiac medications
Coordinate multidisciplinary care between cardiology and obstetrics
Counsel about breastfeeding limitations with cardiac medications
Discuss future pregnancy implications

osces.title: Myocarditis - Viral Cardiomyopathy Post-Respiratory Infection

clinical_scenario.presenting_complaint: Chest pain and fatigue 2 weeks after flu-like illness
clinical_scenario.history_of_presenting_complaint: James had severe influenza-like symptoms 2 weeks ago with high fever, myalgia and cough lasting 5 days. He returned to work but has developed central chest pain over past 3 days, worse on deep inspiration and lying flat, partially relieved sitting forward. Associated with extreme fatigue, exertional dyspnoea and occasional palpitations. He tried ibuprofen which provided minimal relief. No syncope or pre-syncope. Previously very fit, runs 10km three times weekly but now can't climb stairs without stopping.
clinical_scenario.past_medical_history: Nil significant, Fully vaccinated including COVID-19 and influenza
clinical_scenario.medications: Nil regular, Took ibuprofen 400mg PRN past 2 days
clinical_scenario.social_history: Never smoked, Social drinker 2-3 beers weekly, No illicit drugs, Lives alone, Works from home since COVID
clinical_scenario.family_history: Father has hyperlipidaemia, Mother healthy, No cardiac disease or sudden death

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP not elevated, Normal apex beat, Soft S1, Normal S2, Pericardial friction rub absent, No murmurs
examination_findings.respiratory: Clear lung fields, No crackles or wheeze
examination_findings.peripheral: No peripheral oedema, Warm peripheries, Capillary refill 2 seconds
examination_findings.other: Appears fatigued, No lymphadenopathy, No skin rash

investigations.result: Sinus rhythm 95 bpm, PR interval 180ms, Diffuse ST elevation 1-2mm in leads I, II, V4-V6, No reciprocal changes, No Q waves
1850 ng/L at presentation, 2100 ng/L at 6 hours
68 mg/L
WCC 11.8 x10^9/L with lymphocytosis, Hb 145 g/L, Platelets 320 x10^9/L
LVEF 45%, Mild global hypokinesis, No regional wall motion abnormality, Trivial pericardial effusion, Normal valves
investigations.interpretation: Mild LV systolic dysfunction consistent with myocarditis

investigations.result: Late gadolinium enhancement in subepicardial distribution inferior and lateral walls, T2-weighted images show myocardial oedema, No evidence of ischaemic pattern
investigations.interpretation: Findings diagnostic of acute myocarditis (Lake Louise criteria positive)

investigations.result: Influenza A positive, COVID-19 negative, RSV negative

tasks.task: Explain the diagnosis of viral myocarditis to James
tasks.expected_response: James, you have developed viral myocarditis, which is inflammation of your heart muscle following your recent influenza infection. The virus has triggered an immune response that's causing inflammation in your heart, leading to your chest pain, fatigue and reduced heart pumping function. Your cardiac MRI confirms this diagnosis. Most people with viral myocarditis recover completely with supportive care, though recovery takes several months.

tasks.task: Outline immediate management plan
tasks.expected_response: Admit for cardiac monitoring given troponin elevation and reduced ejection fraction. Stop NSAIDs immediately as they can worsen myocarditis and increase risk of complications. Start colchicine 500 micrograms BD for anti-inflammatory effect without NSAID risks. Begin heart failure therapy with ramipril 2.5mg daily and bisoprolol 1.25mg daily, titrating up as tolerated. Monitor daily ECGs for arrhythmias. Bed rest initially with gradual mobilization. No specific antiviral therapy indicated.

tasks.task: Counsel about exercise restrictions
tasks.expected_response: Exercise restriction is critical for your recovery. You must avoid all competitive sports and moderate-high intensity exercise for at least 6 months from diagnosis. This includes your regular 10km runs. Exercise can trigger fatal arrhythmias in active myocarditis. After 3 months, we'll repeat cardiac MRI and exercise stress test. If these show recovery, you can gradually return to light exercise under supervision. Full return to competitive sports only after normal cardiac function confirmed at 6 months.

tasks.task: Discuss potential complications to monitor
tasks.expected_response: While most recover fully, we need to monitor for complications. These include arrhythmias - any palpitations, dizziness or fainting need urgent review. Progressive heart failure with worsening breathlessness or leg swelling requires immediate assessment. Rarely, fulminant myocarditis can develop requiring intensive care support or even mechanical circulatory support. About 20% develop dilated cardiomyopathy long-term. Warning signs include chest pain, palpitations, syncope, or worsening dyspnoea.

tasks.task: Explain follow-up investigations and monitoring
tasks.expected_response: You'll need regular cardiology follow-up at 2 weeks, 1 month, 3 months and 6 months. Serial echocardiograms will monitor your heart function recovery. Cardiac MRI at 3-6 months assesses myocardial inflammation resolution and scarring. 24-hour Holter monitoring checks for arrhythmias before exercise clearance. Blood tests including troponin and BNP track recovery. If ejection fraction doesn't improve by 3 months, we may consider endomyocardial biopsy to exclude giant cell myocarditis requiring immunosuppression.

tasks.task: Address return to work and lifestyle modifications
tasks.expected_response: You can return to sedentary work from home in 1-2 weeks if symptoms improve. Avoid physical stress and maintain regular sleep patterns to support recovery. No alcohol for at least 3 months as it can worsen myocarditis. Ensure adequate hydration but avoid excessive fluids. Get annual flu and COVID vaccines once recovered to prevent recurrence. Consider psychological support as the activity restrictions and uncertainty can cause anxiety. I'll provide a medical certificate for modified duties.

learning_objectives: Diagnose viral myocarditis using clinical and MRI criteria
Understand contraindication of NSAIDs in myocarditis
Implement appropriate exercise restrictions to prevent sudden cardiac death
Plan systematic follow-up with cardiac imaging
Recognize indications for endomyocardial biopsy

osces.title: Atrial Flutter - Ablation vs Cardioversion Decision

clinical_scenario.presenting_complaint: Palpitations and reduced exercise tolerance for 3 weeks
clinical_scenario.history_of_presenting_complaint: Robert noticed sudden onset rapid regular palpitations 3 weeks ago while gardening. Initially intermittent but now constant. Associated with exertional dyspnoea - previously walked 5km daily, now breathless after 500m. Mild chest tightness on exertion, relieved by rest. No syncope or presyncope. Noticed irregular pulse when checking blood pressure at home. Fatigue has significantly worsened, requiring afternoon naps.
clinical_scenario.past_medical_history: Hypertension diagnosed 10 years ago, Type 2 diabetes for 5 years (HbA1c 7.2%), Hyperlipidaemia, BMI 28
clinical_scenario.medications: Perindopril 8mg daily, Amlodipine 5mg daily, Metformin 1g BD, Atorvastatin 40mg daily
clinical_scenario.social_history: Ex-smoker quit 15 years ago (20 pack-years), Moderate alcohol 2-3 standard drinks daily, Retired 2 years ago, Lives with wife
clinical_scenario.family_history: Father had stroke age 75, Mother had atrial fibrillation, Brother has hypertension

examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP 4cm above sternal angle, Regular tachycardia, Normal S1 S2, No murmurs, No signs of heart failure
examination_findings.peripheral: No peripheral oedema, All pulses palpable

investigations.result: Regular narrow complex tachycardia 150 bpm, Sawtooth flutter waves best seen in leads II, III, aVF at 300 bpm, 2:1 AV conduction, No ST-T changes
investigations.interpretation: Typical atrial flutter with 2:1 AV block

investigations.result: Normal LV systolic function LVEF 60%, Mild LA dilatation 42mm, No valvular abnormality, No LV hypertrophy, PASP 30mmHg
investigations.interpretation: Structurally normal heart with mild left atrial enlargement

investigations.result: TSH 2.1 mIU/L, Free T4 15 pmol/L
Na 140 mmol/L, K 4.2 mmol/L, Mg 0.85 mmol/L, Creatinine 95 umol/L, eGFR 75
18 ng/L
Normal cardiac size, Clear lung fields, No pulmonary congestion

tasks.task: Calculate CHA₂DS₂-VASc score and determine anticoagulation need
tasks.expected_response: Robert's CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is 3: Hypertension (1 point), Diabetes (1 point), Age 62 (1 point). With a score of 3, his annual stroke risk is 3.2% without anticoagulation. According to CSANZ guidelines, anticoagulation is strongly recommended. Atrial flutter carries similar stroke risk to atrial fibrillation. Given no contraindications, I recommend starting a DOAC like apixaban 5mg BD or rivaroxaban 20mg daily, which are PBS-listed for this indication.

tasks.task: Explain immediate rate control strategy
tasks.expected_response: We need to slow your heart rate urgently to improve symptoms. I'll start metoprolol 25mg BD as you have no contraindications. This beta-blocker will slow AV node conduction, reducing ventricular rate to target 80-100 bpm at rest. If inadequate response, we can increase to 50mg BD or add digoxin 125 micrograms daily. Avoid calcium channel blockers like diltiazem while on amlodipine due to additive effects. Monitor BP and heart rate response.

tasks.task: Discuss cardioversion timing and preparation
tasks.expected_response: Since symptoms started 3 weeks ago, we cannot cardiovert immediately due to stroke risk. You need therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks before elective cardioversion, or alternatively a transoesophageal echocardiogram (TOE) to exclude left atrial thrombus for earlier cardioversion. After starting apixaban today, schedule cardioversion in 4 weeks. Continue anticoagulation for minimum 4 weeks post-cardioversion regardless of rhythm, as atrial stunning persists. Success rate is 90% but recurrence common at 50% within one year.

tasks.task: Explain catheter ablation as definitive treatment
tasks.expected_response: Catheter ablation is highly effective for typical atrial flutter with 95% cure rate. It involves inserting catheters via groin veins to create a line of ablation across the cavotricuspid isthmus in your right atrium, blocking the flutter circuit. It's a day procedure under sedation, taking 1-2 hours. Major complications are rare (<1%) including cardiac tamponade or AV block. Given high success rate and low recurrence, CSANZ guidelines recommend ablation as first-line treatment for typical flutter rather than long-term medication.

tasks.task: Compare ablation versus cardioversion options
tasks.expected_response: Cardioversion offers immediate rhythm restoration but 50% recurrence within a year, requiring antiarrhythmic drugs long-term. Ablation has 95% long-term success, potentially eliminating need for rate control medications and reducing anticoagulation duration if you remain in sinus rhythm with low CHA₂DS₂-VASc score. Ablation prevents flutter recurrence but you may still develop atrial fibrillation (20-30% chance) requiring continued monitoring. Given your relatively young age and good health, ablation offers better long-term outcomes. I recommend ablation as definitive treatment.

tasks.task: Outline follow-up plan regardless of treatment choice
tasks.expected_response: Start apixaban 5mg BD today for stroke prevention. Begin metoprolol for rate control with BP and heart rate monitoring. Cardiology review in 2 weeks to assess rate control. If choosing cardioversion, book for 4 weeks post-anticoagulation. If choosing ablation, refer to electrophysiology - waiting list typically 6-8 weeks, continue rate control meanwhile. Post-procedure: ECG and Holter monitoring at 3 months, 6 months, then yearly. Continue anticoagulation based on CHA₂DS₂-VASc score even if successful ablation. Lifestyle: reduce alcohol, weight loss, treat sleep apnoea if present.

learning_objectives: Recognize typical atrial flutter ECG pattern
Calculate CHA₂DS₂-VASc score for anticoagulation decisions
Understand 3-week anticoagulation rule before cardioversion
Compare efficacy of ablation versus cardioversion for atrial flutter
Apply CSANZ guidelines for atrial flutter management
key_clinical_guidelines: CSANZ Position Statement on Atrial Flutter Management 2021
eTG - Cardiovascular: Atrial flutter treatment
NHFA/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines 2018
PBS criteria for DOAC prescribing in atrial flutter

osces.title: Hypertensive Crisis with Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES)

clinical_scenario.presenting_complaint: Severe headache, visual disturbance and confusion
clinical_scenario.history_of_presenting_complaint: Margaret was brought to ED by ambulance after colleagues found her confused at work. She complained of severe occipital headache starting 6 hours ago, described as worst headache of her life. Developed bilateral visual disturbance with blind spots and seeing flashing lights. Two witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizures in ambulance lasting 2 minutes each, terminated with midazolam 5mg IV. Post-ictal confusion persisting. No trauma, neck stiffness or fever. Recently increased work stress with overtime shifts. Stopped taking blood pressure medications 2 weeks ago due to feeling well.
clinical_scenario.past_medical_history: Chronic kidney disease stage 3 (baseline creatinine 150 umol/L), Essential hypertension for 8 years, Previous pre-eclampsia with first pregnancy 20 years ago
clinical_scenario.medications: Previously on irbesartan 300mg daily and amlodipine 10mg daily (self-ceased 2 weeks ago)
clinical_scenario.social_history: Never smoked, No alcohol, No illicit drugs, Divorced, Lives with teenage daughter, High stress job in ICU
clinical_scenario.family_history: Mother had hypertension and stroke age 65, Father died of myocardial infarction age 58, Sister has lupus

examination_findings.neurological: GCS 14 (E4V4M6), Confused but following commands, Bilateral papilloedema on fundoscopy, Visual field defects bilateral temporal fields, Brisk reflexes throughout, Plantars equivocal, No focal motor deficit
examination_findings.cardiovascular: JVP elevated 6cm, Hyperdynamic apex beat, Loud S2, S4 gallop present
examination_findings.other: Alert but disoriented to time, Agitated requiring reassurance

investigations.result: No intracranial haemorrhage, No mass lesion, Subtle bilateral occipital and parietal hypodensities
investigations.interpretation: Changes consistent with vasogenic oedema, suggest MRI for PRES

investigations.result: T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in bilateral parieto-occipital regions, predominantly white matter, No diffusion restriction, Pattern consistent with vasogenic oedema
investigations.interpretation: Classic findings of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES)

investigations.result: Creatinine 285 umol/L, eGFR 18, Urea 22 mmol/L, K 4.8 mmol/L
Protein 3+, Blood 2+, No bacteria
156 ng/L
Sinus tachycardia 102 bpm, LVH by voltage criteria, Strain pattern lateral leads
Cardiomegaly, Pulmonary vascular congestion, Small bilateral pleural effusions

tasks.task: Identify this as hypertensive emergency and explain immediate management priorities
tasks.expected_response: This is a hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage - PRES, acute kidney injury, and cardiac injury. Immediate priorities: Transfer to ICU for arterial line monitoring. Target BP reduction of 20-25% in first hour, so aim for 180-190/110-115 mmHg initially. Too rapid lowering can cause cerebral hypoperfusion. Start IV labetalol infusion 2mg/min with titration every 10 minutes. Alternative is nicardipine infusion. Avoid pure vasodilators like hydralazine which increase intracranial pressure. Continuous neurological monitoring for seizure recurrence.

tasks.task: Explain PRES diagnosis and pathophysiology to medical team
tasks.expected_response: PRES is caused by severe hypertension overwhelming cerebral autoregulation, leading to hyperperfusion, blood-brain barrier breakdown and vasogenic oedema, predominantly in posterior circulation. MRI shows characteristic parieto-occipital white matter oedema without infarction. It's reversible with prompt BP control, hence 'reversible' in the name. Untreated, it can progress to intracranial haemorrhage or permanent infarction. Triggers include hypertensive crisis, pre-eclampsia, immunosuppressants, and renal failure - Margaret has both hypertension and CKD.

tasks.task: Outline specific blood pressure targets and timeline
tasks.expected_response: First hour: Reduce MAP by 20-25% (target 180-190/110-115 mmHg) using IV labetalol infusion. Hours 2-6: Gradually reduce to 160/100-110 mmHg if tolerating well and neurologically stable. Within 24-48 hours: Target 140-150/90-95 mmHg. Transition to oral agents when stable - restart irbesartan and amlodipine with dose adjustment for renal function. Long-term target <130/80 given CKD. Monitor for signs of hypoperfusion - worsening confusion, focal deficits, or oliguria indicate too rapid reduction.

tasks.task: Manage seizure risk and provide neuroprotection
tasks.expected_response: Start levetiracetam 1g IV loading then 500mg BD for seizure prophylaxis - renally adjusted dose given eGFR 18. Avoid phenytoin as it's less effective in PRES. Maintain magnesium >1.0 mmol/L as hypomagnesaemia lowers seizure threshold - give 10mmol IV if low. Continuous EEG monitoring for 24 hours to detect non-convulsive seizures. Avoid benzodiazepines unless active seizures. Most patients don't need long-term anticonvulsants - can wean after PRES resolves (typically 2-4 weeks).

tasks.task: Address acute kidney injury management
tasks.expected_response: Margaret has acute on chronic kidney disease - creatinine doubled from baseline. Likely acute tubular necrosis from malignant hypertension. Strict fluid balance with input/output charting. Daily weights. Avoid nephrotoxins - no NSAIDs, contrast, aminoglycosides. May need temporary dialysis if develops oliguria, hyperkalaemia >6.0, acidosis, or fluid overload unresponsive to diuretics. Renal function should improve with BP control. Frusemide 80mg IV for pulmonary oedema if urine output adequate. Nephrology consultation for dialysis planning if no improvement in 24-48 hours.

tasks.task: Discuss prognosis and discharge planning
tasks.expected_response: PRES is reversible in 70-90% with prompt treatment - neurological symptoms typically resolve within days to weeks. MRI changes resolve over 2-4 weeks. Medication adherence is critical - arrange Webster packs and home BP monitoring. Nephrology follow-up for CKD management. Neurology review with repeat MRI in 4 weeks. Address psychosocial stressors - social work referral for workplace stress management. Education about hypertensive emergency warning signs: severe headache, visual changes, confusion need immediate ED presentation. Consider cardiac echo given troponin rise.

learning_objectives: Recognize hypertensive emergency versus urgency
Understand PRES pathophysiology and MRI findings
Apply appropriate BP reduction targets to avoid hypoperfusion
Select appropriate antihypertensive agents for neurological emergency
Coordinate multisystem management in hypertensive crisis

osces.title: Long QT Syndrome - Torsades de Pointes Prevention

clinical_scenario.history_of_presenting_complaint: Emily had sudden loss of consciousness while sitting her pharmacology exam this morning. Witnesses describe 30 seconds of unconsciousness with brief jerking movements. Rapid complete recovery without confusion. She reports feeling heart racing then dizzy before fainting. Similar episode 6 months ago during viva examination attributed to vasovagal. Also describes occasional palpitations during emotional stress or when startled. No chest pain, dyspnoea at rest, or orthostatic symptoms. Recently started azithromycin for sinusitis 2 days ago.
clinical_scenario.past_medical_history: Anxiety disorder, Irritable bowel syndrome, Recent sinusitis
clinical_scenario.medications: Azithromycin 500mg daily (day 2 of 3), Escitalopram 10mg daily for 3 months, Buscopan PRN
clinical_scenario.social_history: Never smoked, No alcohol, No illicit drugs, High stress with final year studies, Lives in student accommodation
clinical_scenario.family_history: Maternal uncle died suddenly age 28 while swimming - presumed drowning, Mother has 'heart rhythm problem' takes medication, Father healthy, Brother aged 20 healthy

examination_findings.cardiovascular: Normal apex beat, Normal S1 S2, No murmurs, No signs of heart failure
examination_findings.neurological: Alert and oriented, Normal neurological examination, No focal deficits

investigations.result: Sinus rhythm 65 bpm, QTc 485ms (Bazett formula), Notched T waves in precordial leads, No ST changes
investigations.interpretation: Prolonged QTc interval (>480ms in females), T wave abnormalities suggestive of long QT syndrome

investigations.result: K 3.9 mmol/L, Mg 0.82 mmol/L, Ca 2.35 mmol/L, Na 140 mmol/L
Normal LV function, No structural abnormality, Normal valves
Average QTc 478ms, Maximum QTc 510ms during emotional stress, 3 runs non-sustained VT (3-5 beats) during sleep
investigations.interpretation: Persistently prolonged QTc with short runs of VT

investigations.result: QTc prolongation to 520ms at peak exercise, Failure to shorten appropriately with heart rate increase, 4-beat run polymorphic VT at recovery
investigations.interpretation: Abnormal QT adaptation and exercise-induced ventricular arrhythmia

investigations.result: Mother: QTc 475ms, Brother: QTc 495ms
investigations.interpretation: Family members have borderline/prolonged QTc suggesting inherited long QT syndrome

tasks.task: Calculate corrected QT interval and explain significance
tasks.expected_response: Using Bazett formula: QTc = QT/√RR interval. With QT 485ms at heart rate 65, the corrected QT is 485ms, which is prolonged (normal <460ms in females). This prolongation predisposes to torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia that can degenerate to ventricular fibrillation causing sudden cardiac death. Your symptoms during stress suggest adrenergic-triggered arrhythmias, typical of long QT syndrome type 1. The risk is increased by QT-prolonging medications like azithromycin and escitalopram you're currently taking.

tasks.task: Identify and manage QT-prolonging medications
tasks.expected_response: Stop azithromycin immediately - macrolides significantly prolong QT. Replace with amoxicillin 500mg TDS for sinusitis. Escitalopram also prolongs QT - discuss with psychiatrist about switching to sertraline which has minimal QT effect. Avoid all high-risk medications: macrolides, fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics (haloperidol, quetiapine), antiarrhythmics (sotalol, amiodarone), antiemetics (ondansetron, domperidone). Check www.crediblemeds.org for comprehensive list. Always inform healthcare providers about your long QT syndrome before prescriptions.

tasks.task: Explain beta-blocker therapy for long QT syndrome
tasks.expected_response: Beta-blockers are first-line therapy for long QT syndrome, reducing cardiac events by 70%. Nadolol 40-80mg daily or propranolol 40mg TDS are preferred - better evidence than metoprolol. They prevent adrenergic-triggered arrhythmias by blunting sympathetic stimulation. Start nadolol 40mg daily, titrating to resting heart rate 50-60 bpm. Never miss doses as withdrawal increases arrhythmia risk. Continue even if asymptomatic. Contraindicated: asthma, severe bradycardia. Side effects: fatigue, cold peripheries, vivid dreams. Beta-blockers are lifelong therapy.

tasks.task: Discuss lifestyle modifications and trigger avoidance
tasks.expected_response: Avoid sudden loud noises (alarm clocks, phones) - use gradual wake alarms. No competitive sports or swimming alone - risk of drowning if arrhythmia occurs. Avoid strenuous exercise but moderate activity is safe. Maintain normal potassium (>4.0) and magnesium (>0.85) - supplement if needed. Avoid energy drinks, excessive caffeine, and stimulants. Manage stress with counseling and relaxation techniques. Medical alert bracelet essential. Inform all healthcare providers, dentists about condition. Genetic counseling before pregnancy - 50% inheritance risk.

tasks.task: Explain indications for ICD implantation
tasks.expected_response: ICD indicated for: recurrent syncope despite beta-blockers, cardiac arrest survivors, torsades de pointes documented, QTc >500ms with symptoms. You meet criteria with QTc 485ms, exercise-induced VT, and syncope. ICD provides backup protection - detects and terminates ventricular arrhythmias. Doesn't replace beta-blockers, used together. Subcutaneous ICD option for young patients avoids transvenous leads. Complications: infection 1-2%, inappropriate shocks 20%, lead problems. MRI compatibility with newer models. Driving restrictions 6 months post-implant.

tasks.task: Arrange family screening and genetic testing
tasks.expected_response: First-degree relatives need ECG screening - your mother and brother already show QT prolongation and need cardiology assessment. Genetic testing can identify specific mutation in 75% of cases - helps risk stratification and guides therapy. LQT1 (swimming triggers), LQT2 (auditory triggers), LQT3 (sleep triggers) have different management. Positive genetic test allows predictive testing of asymptomatic relatives. PBS funds genetic testing with clinical long QT diagnosis. Family members with prolonged QT need beta-blockers even if asymptomatic. Genetic counseling helps understand inheritance pattern and reproductive options.

learning_objectives: Calculate corrected QT interval using Bazett formula
Identify QT-prolonging medications requiring avoidance
Understand beta-blocker therapy as first-line treatment
Recognize ICD indications in high-risk long QT syndrome
Implement family cascade screening for inherited arrhythmia

Heart Rhythm Society Expert Consensus on Long QT Syndrome 2021
